claim: Natural killer (NK) cells play a critical role in limiting tumor growth.
source: Natural killer (NK) cells are lymphocytes of the innate immune system that play a critical role in limiting tumor growth (Vivier et al., 2011; Marcus et al., 2014; Mittal et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Vivier et al., 2011; Marcus et al., 2014; Mittal et al., 2014).

claim: NK cell activation is controlled by a balance of signals from activating and inhibitory receptors.
source: NK cell activation is controlled by a balance of signals from activating and inhibitory receptors, which recognize cognate ligands expressed by potential target cells (Vivier et al., 2011; Shifrin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Vivier et al., 2011; Shifrin et al., 2014).

claim: NKG2D is one of the best-studied NK-activating receptors.
source: One of the best-studied NK-activating receptors is NKG2D, which is also expressed on certain subsets of T cells (Raulet, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Raulet, 2003).

claim: NKG2D is expressed on certain subsets of T cells.
source: One of the best-studied NK-activating receptors is NKG2D, which is also expressed on certain subsets of T cells (Raulet, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Raulet, 2003).

claim: Engagement of NKG2D by its ligands leads to NK cell activation, cytokine secretion, and lysis of target cells.
source: Engagement of NKG2D by its ligands displayed on a target cell membrane leads to NK cell activation, cytokine secretion, and lysis of target cells, such as tumor cells.
evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus about NKG2D function.

claim: NKG2D ligands are structurally similar to MHC Class I proteins.
source: NKG2D recognizes a family of ligands that are structurally similar to MHC Class I proteins.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about NKG2D ligand structure.

claim: Humans express up to eight NKG2D ligands (ULBP1-6, MICA, and MICB).
source: Humans express up to eight NKG2D ligands (ULBP1-6, MICA, and MICB), and mice express 5–6 different ligands, depending on the strain (RAE-1α-ε, H60a-c, and MULT1) (Raulet et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Raulet et al., 2013).

claim: Mice express 5-6 different NKG2D ligands depending on the strain.
source: Humans express up to eight NKG2D ligands (ULBP1-6, MICA, and MICB), and mice express 5–6 different ligands, depending on the strain (RAE-1α-ε, H60a-c, and MULT1) (Raulet et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Raulet et al., 2013).

claim: Healthy cells typically do not display NKG2D ligands on their surface.
source: Healthy cells typically do not display NKG2D ligands on their surface and are thus poor targets for NKG2D-mediated lysis by NK cells.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about NKG2D ligand expression patterns.

claim: Cellular stresses associated with transformation, viral infection, or other danger cause upregulation of NKG2D ligand expression.
source: However, cellular stresses associated with transformation, viral infection, or other danger to the host cause the upregulation of NKG2D ligand expression (Raulet et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Raulet et al., 2013).

claim: Primary tumors and cancer cell lines frequently express one or more NKG2D ligand.
source: Primary tumors and cancer cell lines frequently express one or more NKG2D ligand, and NKG2D expression is important for the control of tumors in vivo in models of spontaneous cancer (Guerra et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Guerra et al., 2008).

claim: NKG2D expression is important for the control of tumors in vivo in models of spontaneous cancer.
source: Primary tumors and cancer cell lines frequently express one or more NKG2D ligand, and NKG2D expression is important for the control of tumors in vivo in models of spontaneous cancer (Guerra et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Guerra et al., 2008).

claim: One mechanism of tumor immune evasion is the loss or decreased expression of NKG2D ligands.
source: In the case of NKG2D-mediated tumor recognition, published results suggest that one mechanism of tumor immune evasion is the loss or decreased expression of NKG2D ligands (Guerra et al., 2008; McGilvray et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Guerra et al., 2008; McGilvray et al., 2009).

claim: Some tumors progress despite sustained expression of NKG2D ligands.
source: In other cases, tumors progress despite sustained expression of NKG2D ligands (Vetter et al., 2002; Guerra et al., 2008; McGilvray et al., 2009; Hilpert et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Vetter et al., 2002; Guerra et al., 2008; McGilvray et al., 2009; Hilpert et al., 2012).

claim: The DNA damage response pathway is implicated in the regulation of one or more NKG2D ligands.
source: Such approaches have implicated the DNA damage response pathway (Gasser et al., 2005), heat shock (Venkataraman et al., 2007; Nice et al., 2009), hyperproliferation (Jung et al., 2012), and pattern recognition receptors (Hamerman et al., 2004), among others, in the regulation of one or more NKG2D ligands.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Gasser et al., 2005).

claim: Heat shock is implicated in the regulation of one or more NKG2D ligands.
source: Such approaches have implicated the DNA damage response pathway (Gasser et al., 2005), heat shock (Venkataraman et al., 2007; Nice et al., 2009), hyperproliferation (Jung et al., 2012), and pattern recognition receptors (Hamerman et al., 2004), among others, in the regulation of one or more NKG2D ligands.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Venkataraman et al., 2007; Nice et al., 2009).

claim: Hyperproliferation is implicated in the regulation of one or more NKG2D ligands.
source: Such approaches have implicated the DNA damage response pathway (Gasser et al., 2005), heat shock (Venkataraman et al., 2007; Nice et al., 2009), hyperproliferation (Jung et al., 2012), and pattern recognition receptors (Hamerman et al., 2004), among others, in the regulation of one or more NKG2D ligands.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Jung et al., 2012).

claim: Pattern recognition receptors are implicated in the regulation of one or more NKG2D ligands.
source: Such approaches have implicated the DNA damage response pathway (Gasser et al., 2005), heat shock (Venkataraman et al., 2007; Nice et al., 2009), hyperproliferation (Jung et al., 2012), and pattern recognition receptors (Hamerman et al., 2004), among others, in the regulation of one or more NKG2D ligands.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Hamerman et al., 2004).

claim: Inhibiting the DNA damage response pathway only partially inhibits NKG2D ligand expression.
source: For example, the DNA damage response is active in many cancer cells and tumor cell lines, but inhibiting that pathway only partially inhibits ligand expression (Gasser et al., 2005; Gasser and Raulet, 2006; Soriani et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Gasser et al., 2005; Gasser and Raulet, 2006; Soriani et al., 2014).

claim: Blocking proliferation does not completely eliminate NKG2D ligand expression by tumor cell lines.
source: Similarly, hyperproliferation can drive NKG2D ligand expression, but blocking proliferation does not completely eliminate NKG2D ligand expression by tumor cell lines (Jung et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Jung et al., 2012).

claim: A genome-wide loss-of-expression mutant screen was performed in the HAP1 cell line to identify novel drivers of NKG2D ligand expression.
source: To identify novel drivers of NKG2D ligand expression, we performed a genome-wide loss-of-expression mutant screen in the tumor-derived human cell line HAP1 (Carette et al., 2009; Carette et al., 2011) and used CRISPR/Cas9 gene targeting methodology for confirmation of the hits and extension of the results.
evidence: Describes the experimental approach used in this study.

claim: HAP1 cells express multiple NKG2D ligands.
source: Like many cell lines, HAP1 cells express multiple NKG2D ligands (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ULBP1 showed the brightest staining on HAP1 cells among NKG2D ligands.
source: We chose to screen for drivers of ULBP1 expression because it showed the brightest staining on HAP1 cells, making it particularly amenable to our loss-of-expression screen.
evidence: Based on experimental observation of staining intensity.

claim: The ULBP1 gene itself was a highly significant hit in the screen.
source: The ULBP1 gene itself was a highly significant hit, providing a validation of this approach.
evidence: Supported by the screen results shown in Table 1.

claim: ATF4 is a stress-associated transcription factor that regulates ULBP1 expression.
source: We chose hits for validation and follow-up experiments based on their statistical ranking and expectations that the corresponding proteins play roles in stress responses, protein biogenesis, or gene/mRNA regulation. The genes chosen encode ATF4 (a stress-associated transcription factor), RBM4 (an RNA-binding protein), HSPA13 (a protein chaperone), and SPCS1 and SPCS2, which are both non-catalytic subunits of the signal peptidase complex.
evidence: ATF4 was identified in the screen and characterized in subsequent experiments.

claim: RBM4 is an RNA-binding protein that regulates ULBP1 expression.
source: We chose hits for validation and follow-up experiments based on their statistical ranking and expectations that the corresponding proteins play roles in stress responses, protein biogenesis, or gene/mRNA regulation. The genes chosen encode ATF4 (a stress-associated transcription factor), RBM4 (an RNA-binding protein), HSPA13 (a protein chaperone), and SPCS1 and SPCS2, which are both non-catalytic subunits of the signal peptidase complex.
evidence: RBM4 was identified in the screen and characterized in subsequent experiments.

claim: HSPA13 is a protein chaperone that regulates ULBP1 expression.
source: We chose hits for validation and follow-up experiments based on their statistical ranking and expectations that the corresponding proteins play roles in stress responses, protein biogenesis, or gene/mRNA regulation. The genes chosen encode ATF4 (a stress-associated transcription factor), RBM4 (an RNA-binding protein), HSPA13 (a protein chaperone), and SPCS1 and SPCS2, which are both non-catalytic subunits of the signal peptidase complex.
evidence: HSPA13 was identified in the screen and characterized in subsequent experiments.

claim: SPCS1 and SPCS2 are non-catalytic subunits of the signal peptidase complex that regulate ULBP1 expression.
source: We chose hits for validation and follow-up experiments based on their statistical ranking and expectations that the corresponding proteins play roles in stress responses, protein biogenesis, or gene/mRNA regulation. The genes chosen encode ATF4 (a stress-associated transcription factor), RBM4 (an RNA-binding protein), HSPA13 (a protein chaperone), and SPCS1 and SPCS2, which are both non-catalytic subunits of the signal peptidase complex.
evidence: SPCS1 and SPCS2 were identified in the screen and characterized in subsequent experiments.

claim: Mutations in ATF4, RBM4, HSPA13, SPCS1, and SPCS2 each resulted in a partial decrease in cell surface expression of ULBP1.
source: Cells with a ULBP1 mutation lacked cell surface ULBP1 staining altogether, as expected, whereas the other mutations analyzed resulted in a partial (twofold to threefold) decrease in cell surface expression of ULBP1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The effect of each mutation was specific to ULBP1 among the NKG2D ligands tested.
source: The effect of each mutation was specific to ULBP1, as we found no change in cell surface expression of other proteins, including four other NKG2D ligands (ULBP2, ULBP3, MICA, and MICB), HLA Class I, the unrelated GPI-anchored protein CD59, or PVR and Nectin-2, the ligands for DNAM-1, another NK cell-activating receptor (Figure 2B,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: ULBP1 expression on mutant lines could be restored by re-expressing the gene of interest with a doxycycline-inducible lentiviral vector.
source: In all cases, ULBP1 expression on mutant lines could be restored by re-expressing the gene of interest with a doxycycline-inducible lentiviral vector (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ATF4 and RBM4 KO cells each showed decreased amounts of canonically spliced ULBP1 mRNA.
source: Consistent with their presumptive roles in gene expression and/or splicing, ATF4 and RBM4 KO cells each showed decreased amounts of canonically spliced ULBP1 mRNA commensurate with the change in cell surface expression (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: HSPA13, SPCS1, and SPCS2 KO cells all showed WT amounts of ULBP1 mRNA.
source: Consistent with their roles as chaperones and protein-processing components, HSPA13, SPCS1, and SPCS2 KO cells all showed WT amounts of ULBP1 mRNA.
evidence: Supported by experimental data (implied from Figure 2E).

claim: Stepwise decreases in ULBP1 expression were observed with each additional mutation in double and triple-mutant cell lines.
source: Notably, we observed stepwise decreases in ULBP1 expression with each additional mutation, with triple-mutant cells showing up to a 20-fold reduction in ULBP1 expression compared to WT cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The genes tested contribute largely independently to steady-state ULBP1 expression in HAP1 cells.
source: These data suggested that the genes tested (with the likely exception of SPCS1 vs SPCS2) contribute largely independently to steady-state ULBP1 expression in HAP1 cells and support a model in which constitutive NKG2D ligand expression in cell lines is due, at least in some instances, to the contribution of several pathways that act cumulatively.
evidence: Based on inference from the stepwise reduction data in Figure 3A.

claim: ATF4/RBM4 double mutants showed a larger decrease in canonically spliced ULBP1 mRNA than either single mutant.
source: ATF4/RBM4 double mutants showed a larger decrease in canonically spliced ULBP1 mRNA than either single mutant, suggesting that ATF4 and RBM4 may act independently in regulating the amounts of ULBP1 mRNA (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ATF4 and RBM4 may act independently in regulating the amounts of ULBP1 mRNA.
source: ATF4/RBM4 double mutants showed a larger decrease in canonically spliced ULBP1 mRNA than either single mutant, suggesting that ATF4 and RBM4 may act independently in regulating the amounts of ULBP1 mRNA (Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on inference from the additive effect observed in double mutants.

claim: Mutation of ATF4 in K-562 cells resulted in the complete disappearance of ULBP1 from the cell surface.
source: WT K-562 cells had relatively low ULBP1 expression, and mutation of ATF4 resulted in the complete disappearance of ULBP1 from the cell surface, as well as an 11-fold reduction in ULBP1 mRNA (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Mutation of ATF4 in K-562 cells resulted in an 11-fold reduction in ULBP1 mRNA.
source: WT K-562 cells had relatively low ULBP1 expression, and mutation of ATF4 resulted in the complete disappearance of ULBP1 from the cell surface, as well as an 11-fold reduction in ULBP1 mRNA (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ATF4-deficiency in Jurkat cells resulted in a modest reduction in ULBP1 mRNA and a barely detectable reduction in ULBP1 cell surface staining.
source: In contrast, ATF4-deficiency in Jurkat cells resulted in a modest reduction in ULBP1 mRNA and a barely detectable reduction in ULBP1 cell surface staining.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: ATF4 drives basal ULBP1 expression in multiple tumor cell lines.
source: The results suggest that ATF4 drives basal ULBP1 expression in multiple tumor cell lines, perhaps reflecting constitutive activation of underlying stress pathways.
evidence: Based on inference from data across multiple cell lines (K-562, HAP1, Jurkat).

claim: ATF4 is induced in a variety of stress conditions including amino acid starvation, the unfolded protein response, oxidative stress, and the presence of dsRNA.
source: ATF4 is induced in a variety of stress conditions that arise in unhealthy, infected, and transformed cells; coupling these stress conditions to NKG2D ligand expression may enable destruction of undesirable cells. Such stresses, including amino acid starvation, the unfolded protein response (UPR), oxidative stress, and the presence of dsRNA, induce ATF4 through phosphorylation of the translation initiation factor eIF2α (Rutkowski and Kaufman, 2003; Suragani et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Rutkowski and Kaufman, 2003; Suragani et al., 2012).

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α globally suppresses protein translation but selectively activates the translation of ATF4.
source: Phosphorylation of eIF2α globally suppresses protein translation but selectively activates the translation of ATF4 (Harding et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Harding et al., 2000).

claim: The transcriptional targets of ATF4 include amino acid transporters and protein chaperones.
source: The transcriptional targets of ATF4 include amino acid transporters and protein chaperones, which in combination with the overall reduction in protein synthesis help mitigate the cellular stress (Harding et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Harding et al., 2003).

claim: ATF4 expression drives the expression of the pro-apoptotic transcription factor CHOP.
source: However, ATF4 expression also drives the expression of the pro-apoptotic transcription factor CHOP (GADD153), suggesting that ATF4 not only drives adaptation to stress but also promotes cell death if the stress cannot be overcome (Tabas and Ron, 2011; Han et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Tabas and Ron, 2011; Han et al., 2013).

claim: Increased ATF4 expression has been detected in some tumors.
source: Increased ATF4 expression has been detected in some tumors (Bi et al., 2005), providing a possible mechanism for coupling malignant transformation to expression of ULBP1, and consequently to tumor immunosurveillance.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Bi et al., 2005).

claim: Histidinol or thapsigargin treatment each significantly induced ULBP1 mRNA in WT K-562, HAP1, and Jurkat cells.
source: Histidinol or thapsigargin treatment each significantly induced ULBP1 mRNA in WT K-562, HAP1, and Jurkat cells, but induction was abrogated or severely blunted when cells lacked ATF4 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Induction of ULBP1 mRNA by histidinol or thapsigargin was abrogated or severely blunted in ATF4-mutant cells.
source: Histidinol or thapsigargin treatment each significantly induced ULBP1 mRNA in WT K-562, HAP1, and Jurkat cells, but induction was abrogated or severely blunted when cells lacked ATF4 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Induction of ULBP1 transcription by the proteasome inhibitor MG132 was not prevented in ATF4-mutant cells.
source: Induction of ULBP1 transcription by the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Butler et al., 2009) was not prevented in the ATF4-mutant cells (data not shown), indicating that certain cellular perturbations transcriptionally activate ULBP1 independently of ATF4.
evidence: Supported by experimental data (not shown in manuscript).

claim: Histidinol treatment caused an increase in ULBP2 mRNA that was partially ATF4-dependent.
source: RT-qPCR analysis of other NKG2D ligands expressed by HAP1 cells showed that histidinol treatment caused an increase in ULBP2 mRNA that was partially ATF4-dependent, while MICA expression was slightly decreased in an ATF4-independent manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: MICA expression was slightly decreased by histidinol treatment in an ATF4-independent manner.
source: RT-qPCR analysis of other NKG2D ligands expressed by HAP1 cells showed that histidinol treatment caused an increase in ULBP2 mRNA that was partially ATF4-dependent, while MICA expression was slightly decreased in an ATF4-independent manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: ULBP3 and MICB transcripts were not affected by histidinol treatment or loss of ATF4.
source: ULBP3 and MICB transcripts were not affected by histidinol treatment or loss of ATF4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ATF4-mediated stress response induces expression of ULBP1, and to a minor extent ULBP2, but not most other NKG2D ligands.
source: These data suggest that the ATF4-mediated stress response induces expression of ULBP1, and to a minor extent ULBP2, but not most other NKG2D ligands.
evidence: Based on inference from the differential effects on various NKG2D ligands.

claim: In K-562 cells, histidinol treatment caused a dramatic ATF4-dependent induction of cell surface ULBP1.
source: Nevertheless, in K-562 cells, we observed a dramatic ATF4-dependent induction of cell surface ULBP1 by histidinol (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and 5D.

claim: In HAP1 and Jurkat cells, histidinol treatment induced ULBP1 cell surface expression slightly in WT cells but caused decreased ULBP1 expression in ATF4-mutant cells.
source: In HAP1 and Jurkat cells, in contrast, addition of histidinol induced ULBP1 cell surface expression slightly in WT cells, but caused decreased ULBP1 expression in ATF4-mutant cells (Figure 5B,D), consistent with the aforementioned inhibition of protein synthesis resulting from histidinol treatments.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and 5D.

claim: Histidinol treatments resulted in substantially decreased cell surface expression of HLA proteins.
source: Indeed, histidinol treatments resulted in substantially decreased cell surface expression of HLA proteins, which are not regulated by ATF4 (Figure 5C,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and 5E.

claim: The overall effect of ATF4 induction by histidinol was to induce and/or maintain ULBP1 cell surface expression in the face of global protein synthesis inhibition.
source: As summarized in Figure 5D, the overall effect of ATF4 induction by histidinol was to induce and/or maintain ULBP1 cell surface expression in the face of global protein synthesis inhibition associated with this stress pathway.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined data on ULBP1 and HLA expression.

claim: ATF4 binds to the ULBP1 promoter in histidinol-treated HAP1 cells.
source: ChIP-Seq with three independent ATF4 antibodies showed a strong peak of ATF4 binding associated with the ULBP1 promoter, along with a smaller peak ∼27 kb downstream in the intergenic region, which could function as an enhancer.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ATF4 binds to a site approximately 27 kb downstream of the ULBP1 promoter in the intergenic region.
source: ChIP-Seq with three independent ATF4 antibodies showed a strong peak of ATF4 binding associated with the ULBP1 promoter, along with a smaller peak ∼27 kb downstream in the intergenic region, which could function as an enhancer.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: No notable ATF4 binding was observed in genes encoding five other functional NKG2D ligands (ULBP2-6).
source: No other notable ATF4 binding was observed in the 266 kb interval shown, which includes genes encoding five other functional NKG2D ligands (ULBP2-6; RAET1K is a pseudogene), at least two of which are expressed in HAP1 cells (ULBP2 and ULBP3) (Figure 6A, data not shown).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The MICA and MICB genes were devoid of ATF4 binding.
source: The MICA and MICB genes were also devoid of ATF4 binding (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq data (not shown in manuscript).

claim: ATF4 binds to the ULBP1 locus in HAP1 cells under steady-state conditions.
source: ATF4 binding at the ULBP1 promoter was confirmed by conventional ChIP-qPCR, which also demonstrated that ATF4 binds to the ULBP1 locus in HAP1 cells under steady-state conditions (no histidinol), and that ATF4 binding is sharply enhanced after histidinol treatment (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D and 6E.

claim: ATF4 binding to the ULBP1 locus is sharply enhanced after histidinol treatment.
source: ATF4 binding at the ULBP1 promoter was confirmed by conventional ChIP-qPCR, which also demonstrated that ATF4 binds to the ULBP1 locus in HAP1 cells under steady-state conditions (no histidinol), and that ATF4 binding is sharply enhanced after histidinol treatment (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D and 6E.

claim: ATF4 overexpression increased ULBP1 promoter activity.
source: ATF4 overexpression increased ULBP1 promoter activity, and the fold-induction was similar for the longer and shorter promoter fragments tested.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutation of the ATF4 motif 138-147 bp upstream of the transcription start site completely ablated promoter activation by ATF4.
source: Mutation of the ATF4 motif 138–147 bp upstream of the transcription start site completely ablated promoter activation by ATF4 (see mutant 1, m1), while mutation of the CRE sites did not reduce induction by ATF4.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutation of the CRE sites did not reduce induction of the ULBP1 promoter by ATF4.
source: Mutation of the ATF4 motif 138–147 bp upstream of the transcription start site completely ablated promoter activation by ATF4 (see mutant 1, m1), while mutation of the CRE sites did not reduce induction by ATF4.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: ATF4 directly transactivates the ULBP1 promoter.
source: We conclude that ATF4 directly transactivates the ULBP1 promoter, and that a single ATF4-binding site drives the bulk of this response.
evidence: Based on inference from ChIP-Seq, ChIP-qPCR, and luciferase reporter assay data.

claim: A single ATF4-binding site drives the bulk of ATF4-mediated ULBP1 promoter activation.
source: We conclude that ATF4 directly transactivates the ULBP1 promoter, and that a single ATF4-binding site drives the bulk of this response.
evidence: Based on inference from the mutagenesis data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: RBM4 is an RNA-binding protein that has been implicated in several steps of gene regulation but has been most studied for its regulation of RNA splicing.
source: RBM4 is an RNA-binding protein that has been implicated in several steps of gene regulation but has been most studied for its regulation of RNA splicing (Markus and Morris, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Markus and Morris, 2009).

claim: A novel isoform of ULBP1 was discovered by RNA-Seq analysis of WT and RBM4 KO HAP1 cells.
source: We compared WT and RBM4 KO HAP1 cells by RNA-Seq to determine a potential role of RBM4 in splicing of ULBP1 transcripts. As a result, we discovered a novel isoform of ULBP1 that to our knowledge has not been previously reported (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Most ULBP1 transcripts in WT cells exhibited the expected splicing pattern to encode the normal ULBP1 protein.
source: Analysis of sequence reads that aligned to splice junctions revealed that most transcripts in WT cells exhibited the expected splicing pattern to encode the normal ULBP1 protein (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: In RBM4 KO cells, approximately 60% of ULBP1 transcripts had undergone an alternative splicing event.
source: In RBM4 KO cells, in contrast, approximately 60% of transcripts had undergone an alternative splicing event of the first and second exons in which the 5ʹ splice site at the 3ʹ border of the first exon was ignored in favor of a 5ʹ splice site located 1.3 kb downstream within the first intron (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The alternatively spliced ULBP1 transcript encodes a premature stop codon shortly after the predicted ER signal peptide.
source: The alternatively spliced transcript in RBM4 KO cells encodes a premature stop codon shortly after the predicted ER signal peptide and is thus unlikely to encode a functional protein fragment (Figure 7C).
evidence: Based on analysis of the sequence of the alternative transcript.

claim: Differential splicing of other NKG2D ligands (MICA, MICB, ULBP2, and ULBP3) was not observed in RBM4 KO cells.
source: We did not observe differential splicing of the other NKG2D ligands expressed by HAP1 cells (MICA, MICB, ULBP2, and ULBP3, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The alternative splicing of ULBP1 transcripts in RBM4 KO cells was confirmed by RT-qPCR analysis.
source: The alternative splicing of ULBP1 transcripts in RBM4 KO cells was confirmed by RT-qPCR analysis (Figure 7C–E, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7C-E and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Canonically spliced ULBP1 transcripts were less abundant in RBM4 KO cells.
source: Canonically spliced ULBP1 transcripts were less abundant in RBM4 KO cells, while the alternatively spliced transcripts were more abundant; the overall abundance of ULBP1 transcripts was unchanged as a result of RBM4-deficiency.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7D-F.

claim: The alternatively spliced ULBP1 transcripts were more abundant in RBM4 KO cells.
source: Canonically spliced ULBP1 transcripts were less abundant in RBM4 KO cells, while the alternatively spliced transcripts were more abundant; the overall abundance of ULBP1 transcripts was unchanged as a result of RBM4-deficiency.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7D-F.

claim: The overall abundance of ULBP1 transcripts was unchanged as a result of RBM4-deficiency.
source: Canonically spliced ULBP1 transcripts were less abundant in RBM4 KO cells, while the alternatively spliced transcripts were more abundant; the overall abundance of ULBP1 transcripts was unchanged as a result of RBM4-deficiency.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: RBM4 impacts cell surface expression of ULBP1 primarily by facilitating the correct splicing of the first two exons of ULBP1 transcripts.
source: The reduction in canonically spliced transcripts was commensurate with the reduction in cell surface ULBP1 protein, suggesting that RBM4 impacts cell surface expression of ULBP1 primarily by facilitating the correct splicing of the first two exons of ULBP1 transcripts.
evidence: Based on inference from the correlation between mRNA and protein levels.

claim: The mutant screen identified several regulators of ULBP1 in HAP1 cells.
source: The mutant screen identified several regulators of ULBP1 in HAP1 cells.
evidence: Summarizes the overall findings of the screen.

claim: Most of the pathways studied control different steps in the biogenesis of ULBP1.
source: Overall, the data suggest that most of the pathways studied control different steps in the biogenesis of ULBP1, with ATF4 controlling transcription, RBM4 regulating RNA splicing, and HSPA13, SCPS1, and SPCS2 regulating co-translational or post-translational steps such as protein processing.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined experimental data on different regulators.

claim: Disabling multiple regulators resulted in much more striking reductions in ULBP1 expression than disabling them individually.
source: The power of the CRISPR/Cas9 method to rapidly generate double- and triple-mutant cell lines led to the finding that disabling multiple regulators resulted in much more striking reductions in ULBP1 expression than disabling them individually.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Each regulator contributes incrementally to ULBP1 expression.
source: Thus, each regulator contributes incrementally to ULBP1 expression.
evidence: Based on inference from the stepwise reduction data.

claim: Greater NK-dependent tumor elimination occurs with increasing amounts of cell surface NKG2D ligand.
source: Previously published evidence demonstrated that greater NK-dependent tumor elimination occurs with increasing amounts of cell surface NKG2D ligand (Diefenbach et al., 2001), consistent with the 'threat-level' hypothesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Diefenbach et al., 2001).

claim: ULBP1 was the only NKG2D ligand with substantially altered expression in each mutant HAP1 cell line.
source: When characterizing the phenotypes of our mutant HAP1 cell lines, we were surprised to find that in each case, ULBP1 was the only NKG2D ligand with substantially altered expression, the one exception being an increase in MICB expression observed on HSPA13 KO cells.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Different NKG2D ligands are specialized with respect to their regulatory mechanisms.
source: These data provide strong support for the proposal that different ligands are specialized with respect to their regulatory mechanisms, providing the capacity to respond to specific classes of threats (Raulet et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on inference from the specificity of regulators for ULBP1, supported by citation (Raulet et al., 2013).

claim: The DNA damage response regulates several NKG2D ligands similarly.
source: In contrast, certain other regulatory pathways, such as the DNA damage response, regulate several NKG2D ligands similarly (Gasser et al., 2005; Soriani et al., 2009; Raulet et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Gasser et al., 2005; Soriani et al., 2009; Raulet et al., 2013).

claim: ATF4 binds to two locations at the ULBP1 locus, including the promoter region.
source: A key finding was that ATF4, a mediator of several stress responses, transcriptionally activates ULBP1. The data show that ATF4 binds to two locations at the ULBP1 locus, including the promoter region, that an ATF4 site in the ULBP1 promoter is essential for ATF4-induced transcription, and that ATF4 drives ULBP1 transcription in wild-type cells.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: An ATF4 site in the ULBP1 promoter is essential for ATF4-induced transcription.
source: A key finding was that ATF4, a mediator of several stress responses, transcriptionally activates ULBP1. The data show that ATF4 binds to two locations at the ULBP1 locus, including the promoter region, that an ATF4 site in the ULBP1 promoter is essential for ATF4-induced transcription, and that ATF4 drives ULBP1 transcription in wild-type cells.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: ATF4 drives ULBP1 transcription in wild-type cells.
source: A key finding was that ATF4, a mediator of several stress responses, transcriptionally activates ULBP1. The data show that ATF4 binds to two locations at the ULBP1 locus, including the promoter region, that an ATF4 site in the ULBP1 promoter is essential for ATF4-induced transcription, and that ATF4 drives ULBP1 transcription in wild-type cells.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A and other figures.

claim: ULBP2 transcription may be regulated by a transcription factor that is induced by ATF4.
source: Since ATF4 was not bound to the ULBP2 promoter, we speculate that ULBP2 transcription is regulated by a transcription factor that is induced by ATF4, or that ATF4 binding to the sites in the ULBP1 gene modestly activates the neighboring ULBP2 gene.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observation of ULBP2 induction without direct ATF4 binding.

claim: ATF4 binding to sites in the ULBP1 gene may modestly activate the neighboring ULBP2 gene.
source: Since ATF4 was not bound to the ULBP2 promoter, we speculate that ULBP2 transcription is regulated by a transcription factor that is induced by ATF4, or that ATF4 binding to the sites in the ULBP1 gene modestly activates the neighboring ULBP2 gene.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the genomic proximity of ULBP1 and ULBP2.

claim: Overexpression of UPR components has been found in primary tumors and cell lines derived from breast cancers.
source: This finding has physiological relevance, as overexpression of UPR components has been found in primary tumors and cell lines derived from breast cancers (Fernandez et al., 2000; Fujimoto et al., 2003), hepatocellular carcinomas (Shuda et al., 2003), and multiple myeloma (Reimold et al., 1996; Munshi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Fernandez et al., 2000; Fujimoto et al., 2003).

claim: Overexpression of UPR components has been found in hepatocellular carcinomas.
source: This finding has physiological relevance, as overexpression of UPR components has been found in primary tumors and cell lines derived from breast cancers (Fernandez et al., 2000; Fujimoto et al., 2003), hepatocellular carcinomas (Shuda et al., 2003), and multiple myeloma (Reimold et al., 1996; Munshi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Shuda et al., 2003).

claim: Overexpression of UPR components has been found in multiple myeloma.
source: This finding has physiological relevance, as overexpression of UPR components has been found in primary tumors and cell lines derived from breast cancers (Fernandez et al., 2000; Fujimoto et al., 2003), hepatocellular carcinomas (Shuda et al., 2003), and multiple myeloma (Reimold et al., 1996; Munshi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Reimold et al., 1996; Munshi et al., 2004).

claim: ATF4 expression is highest in hypoxic regions of tumors.
source: Indeed, ATF4 expression is highest in hypoxic regions of tumors (Ameri et al., 2004; Bi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Ameri et al., 2004; Bi et al., 2005).

claim: Upregulation of ULBP1 by ATF4 provides an additional layer of host defense, marking potentially dangerous cells for elimination by the immune system.
source: Upregulation of ULBP1 by ATF4 provides an additional layer of host defense, marking potentially dangerous cells for elimination by the immune system.
evidence: Based on inference from the role of ATF4 in stress responses and ULBP1 in immune recognition.

claim: Viral infection can activate PERK and PKR, which phosphorylate eIF2α and induce ATF4 expression.
source: As mentioned above, ATF4 expression is induced by phosphorylation of eIF2α. Viral infection can activate PERK and PKR, which phosphorylate eIF2α and therefore induce ATF4 expression (Mohr and Sonenberg, 2012; Jheng et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Mohr and Sonenberg, 2012; Jheng et al., 2014).

claim: RBM4 has been implicated in translation and microRNA-mediated gene silencing.
source: RBM4 has also been implicated in other forms of gene regulation, including translation and microRNA-mediated gene silencing (Lin and Tarn, 2009; Uniacke et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Lin and Tarn, 2009; Uniacke et al., 2012).

claim: RBM4 regulates the alternative splicing of numerous cancer-related genes.
source: It was recently reported that RBM4 regulates the alternative splicing of numerous cancer-related genes. Most interesting, in light of our findings, was the finding based on RNA-Seq analysis that RBM4 expression promoted a tumor-suppressive splicing profile (Wang et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Wang et al., 2014a).

claim: RBM4 expression promoted a tumor-suppressive splicing profile.
source: It was recently reported that RBM4 regulates the alternative splicing of numerous cancer-related genes. Most interesting, in light of our findings, was the finding based on RNA-Seq analysis that RBM4 expression promoted a tumor-suppressive splicing profile (Wang et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Wang et al., 2014a).

claim: RBM4 promoted splicing that generated the pro-apoptotic isoform Bcl-xS, at the expense of the anti-apoptotic isoform Bcl-xL.
source: This action occurred in part through the alternative splicing of the BCL2L1 gene (Bcl-x), wherein RBM4 promoted splicing that generated the pro-apoptotic isoform Bcl-xS, at the expense of the anti-apoptotic isoform Bcl-xL.
evidence: Draws from published literature about RBM4 function.

claim: RBM4 promotes tumor suppression by favoring the canonical splicing of ULBP1 mRNA.
source: Our data suggest that RBM4 further promotes tumor suppression by favoring the canonical splicing of ULBP1 mRNA, marking cells for elimination by the immune system.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data on RBM4's role in ULBP1 splicing.

claim: Decreased RBM4 expression has been observed in various cancers compared to paired healthy tissues.
source: Decreased RBM4 expression has been observed in various cancers compared to paired healthy tissues, including lung, breast, and pancreatic cancers.
evidence: Draws from published literature about RBM4 expression in cancers.

claim: Lower RBM4 expression correlated with decreased patient survival.
source: Furthermore, lower RBM4 expression correlated with decreased patient survival (Wang et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Wang et al., 2014a).

claim: Tumor cells may be under selective pressure to downregulate RBM4 expression.
source: We speculate that tumor cells are under selective pressure to downregulate RBM4 expression, as this would allow tumors to evade tumor-suppressive events such as expression of Bcl-xS and ULBP1.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the tumor-suppressive functions of RBM4.

claim: The subcellular localization of RBM4 is regulated by oxidative stress or activation of the MKK3/6-p38 MAPK pathway.
source: Intriguingly, the subcellular localization of RBM4 is reportedly regulated by oxidative stress or activation of the MKK3/6-p38 MAPK pathway. In that instance, however, stress favored the cytoplasmic localization of RBM4 (Lin et al., 2007), where it reportedly enhanced translation of a subset of mRNAs (Lin et al., 2007; Lin and Tarn, 2009; Uniacke et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Lin et al., 2007; Lin and Tarn, 2009; Uniacke et al., 2012).

claim: HSPA13 belongs to the Hsp70 family of chaperone proteins.
source: HSPA13 (also known as STCH) belongs to the Hsp70 family of chaperone proteins (Otterson et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Otterson et al., 1994).

claim: HSPA13 is associated with microsomes and displays ATPase activity.
source: HSPA13 is associated with microsomes and displays ATPase activity, but little is known about its function, including whether HSPA13 participates in cellular stress responses.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about HSPA13.

claim: HSPA13 binds to the ion transporters NBCe1 and NHE1.
source: One report showed that HSPA13 binds to the ion transporters NBCe1 and NHE1, which help maintain intracellular pH homeostasis (Bae et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Bae et al., 2013).

claim: HSPA13 overexpression increased NBCe1 and NHE1 protein levels and functional activity.
source: HSPA13 overexpression increased NBCe1 and NHE1 protein levels and functional activity.
evidence: Draws from published literature about HSPA13 function.

claim: SPCS1 and SPCS2 are non-catalytic subunits of the signal peptidase complex.
source: SPCS1 and SPCS2 are non-catalytic subunits of the signal peptidase complex, but surprisingly little is known about their function (Mullins et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Mullins et al., 1996).

claim: In yeast, SPCS1 and SPCS2 are required for maximal signal peptidase activity under certain growth conditions.
source: In yeast, SPCS1 and SPCS2 are required for maximal signal peptidase activity under certain growth conditions (Fang et al., 1996; Mullins et al., 1996), and in mammalian cells, SPCS1 supports expression of the HCV protein NS2 (Suzuki et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Fang et al., 1996; Mullins et al., 1996).

claim: In mammalian cells, SPCS1 supports expression of the HCV protein NS2.
source: In yeast, SPCS1 and SPCS2 are required for maximal signal peptidase activity under certain growth conditions (Fang et al., 1996; Mullins et al., 1996), and in mammalian cells, SPCS1 supports expression of the HCV protein NS2 (Suzuki et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Suzuki et al., 2013).

claim: Other transcription factors known to bind the ULBP1 gene and drive gene expression include Sp1, Sp3, and p53.
source: Other transcription factors known to bind the ULBP1 gene and drive gene expression include Sp1, Sp3, and the tumor suppressor protein p53 (López-Soto et al., 2006; Textor et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (López-Soto et al., 2006; Textor et al., 2011).

claim: One or more transcription factors may contribute to ULBP1 transcription in HAP1 and Jurkat cells even after ATF4 is disrupted.
source: It is possible that one or more of these factors contribute to ULBP1 transcription in HAP1 and Jurkat cells, considering that residual ULBP1 expression was observed even after ATF4 was disrupted.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation of residual ULBP1 expression in ATF4 KO cells.

claim: Heat shock, E2F transcription factors, and the DNA damage response drive expression of other NKG2D ligands.
source: Additional stress pathways including heat shock, E2F transcription factors, and the DNA damage response drive expression of other NKG2D ligands, and the combined expression level of all the NKG2D ligands on a given cell will contribute to its ability to activate NK cells (Gasser et al., 2005; Venkataraman et al., 2007; Jung et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Gasser et al., 2005; Venkataraman et al., 2007; Jung et al., 2012).

claim: The combined expression level of all the NKG2D ligands on a given cell will contribute to its ability to activate NK cells.
source: Additional stress pathways including heat shock, E2F transcription factors, and the DNA damage response drive expression of other NKG2D ligands, and the combined expression level of all the NKG2D ligands on a given cell will contribute to its ability to activate NK cells (Gasser et al., 2005; Venkataraman et al., 2007; Jung et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on inference from the cumulative effects of multiple ligands, supported by citations.

claim: HAP1 cells may be representative of a very high 'threat level' as they had activated numerous ULBP1 drivers and independent drivers for several other NKG2D ligands.
source: HAP1 cells may be representative of a very high 'threat level', as they had activated numerous ULBP1 drivers, and independent drivers for several other NKG2D ligands.
evidence: Based on inference from the multiple activated pathways observed in HAP1 cells.

claim: HAP1 cells possessed potent NK-activating properties distinct from NKG2D ligands.
source: Moreover, these cells possessed potent NK-activating properties distinct from NKG2D ligands, as shown by studies with NKG2D-deficient NK cells (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (not shown in manuscript).

claim: Loss of ULBP1 drivers had little detectable effect on the capacity of HAP1 cells to stimulate an NK response.
source: Probably as a consequence, loss of ULBP1 drivers, and even ULBP1 itself, had little detectable effect on the capacity of HAP1 cells to stimulate a response (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (not shown in manuscript).

claim: The layers of ULBP1 regulation could allow NKG2D ligand expression to be fine-tuned to reflect the 'threat level' of the cell.
source: The layers of ULBP1 regulation we have described could allow NKG2D ligand expression to be fine-tuned to reflect the 'threat level' of the cell.
evidence: Based on inference from the multiple independent regulatory pathways identified.

claim: Ubiquitous RBM4 expression is 'safe' for normal, healthy cells, since functional ULBP1 cannot be spliced unless the gene is transcribed in the first place.
source: Ubiquitous RBM4 expression is 'safe' for normal, healthy cells, since functional ULBP1 cannot be spliced unless the gene is transcribed in the first place.
evidence: Based on logical inference about the sequential nature of transcription and splicing.

claim: None of the hits investigated are related to previously known drivers of ULBP1 or other NKG2D ligands.
source: The results of our screen highlight diverse mechanisms for the control of NKG2D ligand expression. To the best of our knowledge, none of the hits we investigated are related to previously known drivers of ULBP1 or other NKG2D ligands, and the effects found were generally specific to ULBP1.
evidence: Based on comparison with published literature and the specificity observed in experiments.

claim: The effects of the identified regulators were generally specific to ULBP1.
source: The results of our screen highlight diverse mechanisms for the control of NKG2D ligand expression. To the best of our knowledge, none of the hits we investigated are related to previously known drivers of ULBP1 or other NKG2D ligands, and the effects found were generally specific to ULBP1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing specificity for ULBP1 in Figure 2 and related figures.
